subject: SLA baseline, latency carveouts and monthly credit construct
messages:
From: Mateo Alvarez <mateo_alvarez@redwood.com>

Cc: Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.com>, Laura Bennett <laura_bennett@redwood.com>, Aditya Rao <aditya_rao@redwood.com>

Subject: SLA baseline and credits — draft attached

Jordan / ApexCare team,

Thanks again for the productive call yesterday. Per our discussion, attaching a focused SLA draft and an illustrative monthly credits matrix so you can see how we map uptime/latency violations to remedy amounts. Key items to review:

- Standard hosted baseline: 99.95% monthly uptime (intent is to balance predictable latency and cost).
- Dedicated option: 99.975% (for customers who reserve capacity).
- Latency SLOs: p95 and p99 windows are defined per-route (we included example thresholds at p95 < 250ms, p99 < 800ms).
- Maintenance/force majeure carveouts and scheduled maintenance windows (we propose a 4-hour monthly maintenance bucket that is not credited).
- Monthly credit formula in the spreadsheet is prorated by percentage of downtime and capped at a percentage of monthly bill (shown as a sliding cap).

Two asks from our side:
1) Confirm whether your procurement team needs a single percent uptime floor (we used 99.95) or a split floor depending on Ded vs Hosted.
2) Any specific operational carveouts you need for batch-heavy workloads (batched inference can create transient latency spikes we can carve out if you prefer).

Attachments: redwood_sla_draft_v2.pdf, uptime-credits-matrix.xlsx

If useful I can schedule a short follow-up with Marissa (legal/ops) and Laura (product) tomorrow.

Best,

Thanks, Mateo — received and skimmed. A couple of quick reactions from procurement and our SRE lead: 

- Uptime: 99.95% for hosted feels OK as a starting point, but we need clarity on how regional incidents are counted for a globally distributed service. Is the uptime measured per-tenant average across regions or per-region?

- Latency credits: Our apps are sensitive to p99 latency more than p95. The credit curve in the spreadsheet is heavily driven by p95 breaches; we'd like p99-triggered credits (even if smaller) because those tail latencies materially impact UX for high-value workflows.

- Maintenance carveouts: A 4-hour monthly maintenance bucket is reasonable, but we need an explicit definition of "scheduled" vs "emergency" maintenance and a notice window. Also request that planned maintenance for our dedicated capacity be scheduled outside our business hours PDT and give 72h notice.

- Cap: The proposed cap looks low relative to our expected business impact. Can you explain rationale? We typically expect at least a 50% monthly credit cap for the first 6 months of a pilot, or an outage severity ladder that scales non-linearly.

Timeline: procurement is targeting a countersign by end of next week if we can converge on uptime wording and the credit cap.

Jordan — thanks for the clear notes. I've reviewed the draft and the matrix and proposed an operational compromise below that addresses your p99 concern and the cap ask while keeping our standard guardrails. High-level proposal: 

1) Measurement scope
- Uptime measured per-tenant and per-region. If your workloads are routed to a single region we will report that region's uptime; for multi-region routing the platform-level uptime is computed per-tenant as the weighted average across regions by request volume. We will include region-specific reporting in the Console and in monthly uptime exports.

2) Latency SLOs & credit triggers
- Primary SLOs: p95 < 250ms, p99 < 800ms (hosted). For Dedicated we set p95 < 200ms, p99 < 650ms.
- Credits will be eligible for sustained breaches: either (A) a daily p99 breach (p99 exceeds threshold for >30% of daily windows) or (B) a monthly aggregated p99 that exceeds threshold by >20% of the allowed budget. This avoids single transient spikes causing full credit events.
- When p99 is breached above thresholds, credit is calculated using a reduced multiplier vs uptime (we propose 0.5x of the uptime-prorated credit for latency-triggered events) to reflect mitigated user impact vs full downtime.

3) Maintenance carveouts
- Scheduled maintenance: calendarized and communicated 72h in advance; any maintenance that meets that notice is exempt up to 4 hours per month.
- Emergency maintenance: defined and limited to safety/security incidents; we will provide a post-incident report and will not count emergency maintenance under scheduled carveouts.

4) Monthly credit cap & pilot accommodation
- Standard cap: 30% of the monthly invoice for hosted, 40% for Dedicated.
- Pilot concession: for an initial 3-month pilot we can raise the cap to 60% (one-time concession) provided volume does not exceed the agreed pilot commitment; after pilot we revert to standard cap.

5) Billing mechanics & payout
- Credits are applied as account credits on the next invoice cycle; if you prefer a cash refund we can discuss for enterprise agreements.

6) Batch inference carve-in
- We will offer a configuration toggle: if you run batched inference patterns that you want carved out, we will exclude that route's p99 from platform-wide latency SLOs and treat it with a separate, agreed threshold.

I've updated uptime-credits-matrix.xlsx to reflect the above — please see the highlighted rows. If that looks acceptable I can have Legal produce a redline for the contract with the pilot cap reflected.

Thanks,
Marissa Cole
Head of Customer Ops, Redwood Inference

Marissa / Mateo — appreciate the fast follow-up and the detailed approach. A few quick items from our side: 

- Measurement per-region and weighted averaging works for our traffic profile. Please make sure the monthly export includes the per-region uptime buckets and per-route p99 distributions.
- The sustained-breach definition for p99 is reasonable; we may ask for the raw percentile windows during contract review but the proposed approach should address product risk.
- The pilot concession (60% cap for 3 months) is acceptable in principle. Procurement will ask for it to be written as: "Pilot Cap: 60% credit cap for the first three paid months of service when customer has signed a pilot commitment (volume threshold defined in SOW)."
- We still want explicit language that scheduled maintenance outside our specified maintenance windows requires prior written consent (e.g., by email from our procurement contact).

Next steps: if you can circulate a legal redline with the pilot clause and the per-region reporting commitment, Procurement can aim to countersign the pilot SOW and get things started next week. Also send the DocuSign link when available.

Thanks — Jordan
